items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: I know there were some in town because was a place not far from where I was working called the Tabou and Wallace Bishop, my ex-drummer, was working there with a British West Indian tenor player named Sammy Walker

ctx.x: I saw the owner of the club once, and that was when we opened. But he was there every night until ten o'clock. The bad business that the place did, didn't seem to worry him. He was the manager of a boxer named Muller who was quite well known in Germany. He would play poker every night in another room until ten, and then he would disappear. The cashier was a woman, and she was in chrage of everything. We worked eight hours and had two fifteen minutes rest periods. And as there was supposed to be continuous music,…

The most that ever came to the joint was one Saturday when there were at least 150 of them at 11 o'clock. At 2'30, the waiters had chased them all away, except a couple of fellows at the bar. At 8p.m. when we went to work, the sun was still shinning, and when we finished at 4.a.m., day was breaking, and the only happy things living seemed to be birds that we heard singing. No one ever came to me and told me that they were jazz fans, and I know there were some in town because was a place not far from where I was…

But we met a nice young couple who was planning to get married soon, Hildchen and Gunter Kwiatkowsky, who invited us in their parents' home and also introduced us to some of their friends. Sometimes, we were invited by some of them or went out in some keller. Colgone had been very heavily bombed and it was quite a sad sight to see.
